Dear Belgravian,

Following A.A.Harley's untimely death last year your Committee considered various proposals for commemmorating the unique service rendered to the Club by this fine Belgravian. It was eventually decided that a Club Honours Board featuring Senior Championship successes was not only something that a club of our stature merited anyway, but it would be particularly appropriate for carrying a plaque in memory of Alf. who took such an interest in the history of our club and its many team successes.

During Alf Harley's 46 years of membership he was twice President, Honorary Secretary for 26 years, Editor for 9 years and Walking Secretary for 10 years, and thousands of Belgravians enjoyed the benefits of his selfless devotion to the Club. There are many, I am sure, who would wish to be associated with this project by contributing to the cost of the board (approximately £270).

The fund has already been launched by the Past Presidents, Vice-Presidents and Life Members of the Club but its success depends also on General membership. Subscribers will be notified of the unveiling date and acknowledged in the December "Belgravian".

Your donation, however small, will be gratefully received by:-

items.heading: COMMENT
items.summary: Editorial on the new all-weather jumping surfaces at Battersea Park, the lack of facilities in south-west London, and athletics as a sport open to anyone.
items.text:
At last Battersea Park athletic track can boast some all-weather surfacing. Well, on the jumping areas at least. The long jump run-up was put down by Dunlop and the high jump area has been laid with a substance developed in the United States and completely new to this country. In the few weeks that these areas have been in use there has already been a noticeable increase in the standard of jumping and in the number of those who wish to jump at Battersea track.

There appear to be no plans afoot to resurface the entire track or to enhance the pole vault and throwing areas. Apparently there is also a problem in safely housing the high jump landing bed, for at the present the only vandal proof store is on the other side of the Park, and this means that it is not always available for use. All this is a great pity because the whole south-western sector of London is very much a barren wasteland as far as the athlete is concerned. He or she must travel to West London Stadium or the Crystal Palace to use the most modern athletic facilities. On the credit side, the groundsman at Battersea has intimated that during the winter months when he is less busy he will cut down the remains of the old pole vault 'mound'(at present inhabited by a nest of rats), so that at least that site will be ready should any developments arise.

On a slightly different tack, a TV programme some weeks ago highlighted the problems faced by youngsters in south-west London. The main point made was that there is nothing for them to do and nowhere for them to go, not even for a kick-about with a football. The fact that a large park exists in Battersea with football pitches, tennis courts and an athletic track, not to mention a fun-fair, riverside embankment and gardens, seemed to be totally ignored by the programme. However, it must be admitted that these amenities are not available on winter evenings, and if a scheme could be got off the ground to develop a sports centre that would be open all year round in all weathers, a great deal would have been done to alleviate the problem. It would certainly also give athletics the chance to exploit an area of London that is virtually untapped.

Our sport has a great advantage over others in that it can be practised by almost anyone who has the determination to get up and have a go. Bear in mind the incredible performance of the man at our league meeting at Exeter who, with only one leg, won the high jump with a leap of 6'0"! Whatever one's sex or shape or size, there is an athletic event to be tackled and even if one is never likely to become a world-beater there is the pleasure of measuring improvements, inch by inch and second by second.

Given the facilities athletics can be a real glamour sport, attracting many more than the comparative few who now take part.

items.heading: grapevine
items.summary: Club gossip column: Ted Stimpson's operation and career, Richard Moody's naval tour, Wilf Wesch judging at Hamburg, the death of Hall caretaker Tom Savage, Leo Coy's ranking lists, John Martin leaving the AAA Championships, births in club families, and short notes on Gordon Biscoe, Dennis McKeown, Paul Whitby, Henry Martin, Paul Williamson and Lionel Mann's Civil Service Marathon win.
items.text:
• TED STIMPSON recently underwent an operation in Wimbledon Hospital and is now out and about again. He was pleased to see a number of Belgravians who visited him during his short stay in hospital. Ted, a Past-President, is one of those who do a great deal for us, lending a hand at track, country and road fixtures. He also plays a large part on our social side and for many years has organised the Club's Annual Dinner - an event which few, if any, clubs can equal. In 1939 he led our cross-country team home in the "National" at Manchester to score our second team win (the first was in 1935), and as fourth man home gained an international vest. After war service he gained another E.C.C.U. winning team medal at Sheffield in 1948. Over recent years he has enjoyed a weekly spin over the Common, and is a regular attender at Committee meetings; he also represents us on the Middlesex County A.A.A. Committee.

• RICHARD MOODY, now a Surgeon Lieutenant in the Royal Navy, is off on an enviable tour of duty this winter. He sails from Plymouth on September 17th on board HMS Achilles, a Leander Class frigate, as Medical Officer for a group of ships. Ports of call will be Gibralta - where he hopes to take part in the race to the top of the rock, Cape Town, Mombasa, Mauritius - for Christmas, and Singapore. Richard will be back in the UK next summer.

• We had a representative at the International Walks at Hamburg in May, the Chief Judge was our Vice-President and Olympic representative WILF WESCH.

• Many years ago when Belgrave Hall was St. John's Hall it was looked after by a Mr. and Mrs. SAVAGE. With the passing of time the Hall became ours, the dear old couple passed on and the good work was carried on for a number of years by their son TOM. We are sorry to learn that Tom died recently in Wimbledon Hospital. For a good many years he cleaned up at the Hall and served us with refreshments, and we mourn the passing of an old friend.

• LEO COY has taken over the job of recording the United Kingdom's Club Ranking lists for the National Union of Track Statisticians. Let us hope that the performances of Belgrave athletes will make his task that much more enjoyable.

• The scene was the A.A.A. Championships. The world record holder and ex-world record holder were engaged in a seven-foot-plus duel in the high jump and three leading American pole vaulters were also in action. ".... Cheerio blokes, I'm going now...." JOHN MARTIN our field events captain was actually leaving right in the middle of such excitement. It has always been said that the call of true love is strong. Poor John must have it bad!

• For two years now PETE SUTTON has been unable to run because of a chipped bone in his foot but it's nice to see him regularly at the Hall on a Sunday morning, keeping in touch even if he can't get out for a jog.

• There seems to have been a population explosion in Belgrave circles recently. PETER and MARGARET HILLIAR and DON and JENNY MacLEAN are hearing the patter of tiny feet ... again. Spectating at the Club Championships was none other than our 800 metre record holder DAVE COCKS with two year old daughter ELIZABETH. Dave and his wife CHRIS (ex-Selsonia) are both well and have recently had another addition to their family - a son GRAHAM. PAM and JOHN DAVIS, another Selsonia Ladies AC/Belgrave partnership, are also doing their best to keep the Club stocked with thoroughbreds, and seven weeks after the arrival of another bouncing boy, Pam was out jogging again.

• A few raised eyebrows were in evidence from visiting officials at the Club Championships when GORDON BISCOE regarded the new all-weather long jump run up and said with tongue in cheek, "Looks good. Should be alright when they get the cinders down on top of it!"

• DENNIS McKEOWN has been away in Belgium for two months racing on his bike with some success. He looks forward to donning his running shoes again in the near future.

• Hurdlers beware! PAUL WHITBY begins a post graduate physical education course at Madeley College this autumn. Hopes to be super-fit next season.

• Making a welcome appearance at our last Battersea track meeting was the incredible HENRY MARTIN who has probably been a member of more athletic clubs than he has had training sessions. Now running in the colours of Hercules Wimbledon, his come-back run over 200 metres was his first race on the track after four years of injury problems.

• PAUL WILLIAMSON is off to Norwich and East Anglia University where he will be studying history and art.

• Congratulations to LIONEL MANN upon winning the Civil Service Marathon Championship held in conjunction with the Poly A.A.A./R.R.C.marathon.

items.text:
.... is probably the word I'm looking for - it's this that makes administration so much easier. It's when someone goes beyond the line of duty, often without being asked, to put themselves out to help our Club. I'm not referring to the Carters, Biscoes, Bakers and Couzens of our Club who frequently receive the accolades they deserve, but to the man often overshadowed. Someone like Pete Sutton who sweeps out the canteen and committee room, someone like Joe McDonald who at the hint of a suggestion is so eager to please, or Fred Paget washing up and running a bar. And talking of bars - Dennis MacManus, Jack Carter and Stuart Barrett - we couldn't have done without them. These are not just words, without them we could have put up the shutters as far as socials were concerned. Brian 'T' Gorman and his efforts have given heart to our training from the Hall. Colin Pearson, an active athlete, has rolled up his sleeves to the most foul but necessary cleaning work. Arthur Penstone, always busy - Bert Stroud with his wife and kids, whether it's in the canteen or standing on corners directing runners for four hours at a stretch and still smiling. To mention one lady makes others immediately spring to mind. Pat Mead, never an observer, always involved, the track people know how much and all who read this magazine owe her thanks. Evelyn Stimpson, mainspring in so many ventures, grafting away with needle and thread or paintbrushes or pottery, forever helpful and understanding. Margaret McMillan and her great efforts at the Bazaar - Sue Coy - Mary Crookes and Stephanie Langheim - have all pitched in with their positive contributions. Gwen Couzens and Bill's Mum at the Jumble Sales. My own Mum, not Yidisha but a continuous source of lucrative ideas and help. And Linda, my bossy daughter, who as I write is making papier mache piggy banks for the Merton Show - her involvement with tea making, distributing leaflets, selling programmes, running raffles, etc., is total.

I thank you all - missed some? Of course. The bloke what never made a mistake never made anything. To those, please accept my apologies. And to you all, cited or not, thank you - thank you very much.

CHAS. MANNING, President.

items.heading: SPOTLIGHT on .......... STEPHEN WHITE
items.summary: Profile of sprinter and jumper Steve White, who joined Belgrave in 1965, with his representative honours and an interview by Alan Mead about his training, motivation and views on Belgrave's future in the Southern and National Leagues.
items.text:
Steve White became a member of Belgrave Harriers as a 15 year old in 1965, introduced by Tony Brooks. Immediately, those connected with the track and field side could not help being impressed by the slim youngster who trained with purpose from the very beginning, who seemed to know exactly what he was about, and who exuded the calm confidence of a future champion.

Nearly a decade later, Steve could be said to be the man at the heart of our team. It's not just that he nearly always wins for us, it's the way he does it with assurance and flowing style, perhaps three or four times during an afternoon. He lives at Oxford and in spite of the travelling involved, always turns out for the Club in league and cup matches. On one occasion this year he had gone down to Brighton for the weekend yet still visited Mayesbrook Park in East London to spearhead our team. Another time, representative honours had been gained by him but there was no easing up for the event as he staunchly carried the claret and gold for us just the day before.

Representative honours include the A.A.A., Southern Counties A.A.A., Surrey A.A.A., Berks/Bucks/Northants/Oxon., and he gained a junior international vest in matches against France and West Germany in 1969. Steve was 3rd in the English Schools senior 200 metres in 1968, 2nd in the junior A.A.A. 200 metres championship in 1969 and a finalist in the senior A.A.A. 200 metres in 1973. He has sprinted faster than any other Belgravian and only John Mitchell has leapt further. Honours are not confined to the sports field, however. At Tulse Hill School he was Deputy Head Boy and has been President of Oxford University Athletic Club.

The following questions were put to Steve recently by Alan Mead and give some insight to the motivation of this quiet, great Belgravian.

Alan: What made you choose athletics as your main sport?
Steve: I suppose I enjoyed the personal success of athletics. It was good to win at football of course but there it's a team success, athletics gave me a lot of personal confidence. Also, I preferred the loneliness of the training, it seemed more purposeful and there was a greater sense of progress than in the team games. This is not to say I spurned company, not that I didn't enjoy team games. It was just that if I was going to take something seriously then I had to devote all my self-centred attention to it; football etc., was an enjoyment, athletics became more fundamental. There was, moreover, the sheer aesthetic pleasure of running well and being fit.

A: Are any other members of your family involved in sport?
S: I think my father used to play football in the Army, otherwise not.

A: How often did you train when you started running and jumping?
S: I started at primary school when I was 9 but that didn't involve much training, I just ran when the district sports came along. I can remember going to Sunday morning training at Tooting Bec prior to the local cub pack's sports - we really were very keen. I didn't start training seriously until I was 14 - about 5 days a week.

A: What other sports did you take part in at Tulse Hill School?
S: Soccer, basketball, cricket for my first two years until athletics began to intrude.

A: A basketball player I once encountered said you were known as "wonderboy" as you were a good all-rounder.
S: It makes me sound like some "All American Boy" cartoon character. I hope nobody called me this, but I certainly was actively involved in three major sports, captain in two of them (athletics and basketball) and particularly successful in athletics, and my successes were well paraded by the school authorities. I suppose it did make me popular and it meant that I got to know a great many people whom I would never normally have spoken to, and they me. For a great many boys at Tulse Hill prowess at sport was more admirable than any other ability.

A: Did you receive any coaching at school?
S: I did receive the regular coaching from school masters until I had some success and showed some promise. I was then singled out for more privileged attention and given more detailed schedules and so on. Then, when I joined Belgrave, there was Dave Ansell who was one of the finest long jump coaches in the country. (I think Derek Cole and Alan Lerwill have missed him since he went North - we all owe a lot to Dave). Then in my fourth year at school, Dick Wyer arrived to teach P.E. and he has been friend and 'coach' ever since.

A: Where did you train at that time?
S: At school, where gymnasium and weights facilities were excellent, plenty of encouragement too; Brockwell Park and Herne Hill track.

A: How much of your early success was due to sheer ability?
S: I honestly don't know because I was training relatively seriously relatively early and therefore never permitted myself to rely for long on natural ability alone. However, I did win races at primary school, at district level and at holiday camps. I suppose actually that natural ability was important and also a contributory factor in my choice of athletics as my main sport. I've tended to be a bit philosophical in my answer to your first question - sheer natural ability was important.

A: What ambitions did you have in those days?
S: In the short run to win the English Schools (I'm still upset that I never did); to win a junior international vest; to pass my exams ('O' and 'A' levels) - this above all else. In the long run to win the Olympics, of course! and to go to University.

A: What were your achievements in sport in your Tulse Hill days?
S: Early on in soccer; in my second year we won the Ewell Trophy and London Grammar School Cup (we were the best team in London that year). I was playing for a Sunday club side which perennially won league and cup. Until I started to play in the 1st eleven, I honestly think the team I was playing in lost no more than 10 matches. That probably had little to do with me but it was marvellous to play in such successful teams. In basketball I played for London Schools. In athletics I won the London Schools Intermediate long jump in 1967, 3rd in the English Schools senior 200 metres 1968, 2nd A.A.A. junior 200 metres, junior internationals against France and West Germany 1969.

A: When did you go up to Oxford and what were you reading?
S: October 1970; Politics, Philosophy and Economics.

SPOTLIGHT ON STEVE WHITE Continued..........

A: How did you make your mark in the athletics team?
S: I actually went up to Oxford assuming I would have no trouble getting into the athletics team and quite honestly I didn't; the standards were not particularly high and anybody who had success at school was eagerly welcomed.

A: When did you become President of Oxford University Athletic Club?
S: In 1973 for academic year 1973-74. My term ended in May this year after the Varsity match. Julian Goater is the present President. I was Hon. Sec. in 1971-72 and have been on the committee in one way or another ever since.

A: You graduated in 1973, how is your post graduate course going?
S: Fairly laboriously at present. I spent much too much time being President of O.U.A.C. last year and now spend hours in the library catching up and trying to find a thread for a thesis. I must admit I'm looking forward to finishing and leaving the academic environment.

A: What do you hope to do after this?
S: "Something in the City". Actually I really don't know specifically, but probably something allied to my subject (Economics). Perhaps Government Economic Service or Bank of England. I do fancy working for the U.N. or something like that but they usually require experience in business or government first. I really don't relish the prospect of becoming an urban commuter with mortgages and gas bills. Perhaps I'll work for 'Shelter' or 'Child Poverty Action" - the irony of that would be that I probably couldn't afford to find accommodation myself. This might all sound a little flippant but I'm not too concerned about my future (I think my wife's more concerned!) and I'm confident I'll do something worthwhile and enjoyable.

A: When did you meet your wife?
S: I met Jean in 1968. We were married in 1972.

A: How does Jean view your athletic career?
S: With benign tolerance.

A: What moments stand out in your athletics?
S: My worst moment is being knocked out of the English Schools 200 metres in 1969 when I had the fastest time in the country to date and was favourite - I really wanted to win that.

I was really pleased on beating Cambridge by a record margin this year, not because the Varsity Match is a prestigious match nowadays, not primarily because of anything I did personally, but because it was such a magnificent team performance and there was a real sense of club spirit. That was a wonderful reward for all the tribulations I experienced as President throughout the year.
Other than this I felt totally elated to break 22 seconds for the first time and 24 feet and also 50 seconds for 400 metres. I've run abroad for Lambeth, Great Britain and O.U.A.C. and I've enjoyed every trip.

A: Have you met many athletic "personalities"?
S: David Hemery once in the showers at Crystal Palace. Alan Pascoe is a "good bloke". Both he and Hemery, I've noticed, are prepared to give encouragement to youngsters, to interrupt their own sessions to say a few words. I really admire such humility in such greatness. But I have met many people in athletics and quite honestly, whether they've been "personalities" or not hasn't really been significant.

A: Do you prefer jumping or sprinting?
S: It depends whether I am jumping or sprinting well. Though I do find it more difficult to train for jumping because of lack of company and coaching at Oxford; it's easier to get out and run.

A: Have you realised your athletic ambitions?
S: I do worry about improving and I do still want to obtain an international vest. But I'm not obsessed with this particular ambition. I will do all I can to achieve it but if I fail I will find satisfaction in the knowledge that I have tried rather than disappointment in failure. More important is to enjoy athletics here and now, and I do, so I have no reason to complain. Doing the O.U.A.C's President's job made me approach the sport from a new direction, and as I have said, creating a club spirit and helping the rest of the team gave me a great deal of enjoyment and satisfaction. I'm sure it is the most worthwhile thing I have done at Oxford.

A: How long will you continue to compete?
S: For as long as I enjoy it. I suspect that when I start work, it might be a case of for as long as I can find the time.

A: Would you be satisfied with competing at a lower level?
S: I often wonder whether my enjoyment of athletics derives from my success. I believe it might. In which case if I cease to be successful I shall cease to enjoy athletics and therefore pack it up. However, my criteria for success might change, I might regard myself as successful if I am fit at 30 and so continue to do athletics even though I am no longer winning. I hope I shall do some sport when I am older. I'm certainly not doing it for the glory and nothing else.

It's 1969 and Steve White, fastest junior in Britain with 21.[illegible], wins the Southern Counties A.A.A. junior 200 m. in 21.8. Photo: Ron Linstead.

SPOTLIGHT ON STEVE WHITE Continued..........

A: How often do you train and what type of training do you do?
S: Six days per week, winter and summer.
Weights three times per week in winter, twice per week in spring and once in summer. I get coaching/advice from Dick Wyer, otherwise I just work things out for myself.
I train mainly at Iffley Road track and sports hall or on college playing fields. My sessions are very flexible and varied to avoid boredom. I usually try to concentrate on one particular aspect of technique per session, leg drive, arms or whatever. I do repetition work over 60, 70, 120, 150, 200, 300 metres and always try to keep the quality high, even in snow. This isn't easy but I prefer This approach to doing, say 10 x 300 metres with 30 seconds recovery in about 45 seconds. Anything above 38 seconds for a 300 metres is poor for me.
I do a lot of supplementary work, stretching, hopping, bounding, weighted belts, etc. In fact, I spend one whole session a week doing this sort of thing in the winter. Weights: I mix pyramid work, in which I go for maximums (215lbs. clean, 210lbs. bench press, 600lbs squat), with light, fast repetitions in order to facilitate speed of contraction and avoid feeling cumbersome.
In general I try to fulfil set tasks but never by strain and unnecessary pain. Relaxation is fundamental, enjoyment is absolutely essential. I couldn't become an athletic metronome. I like to think that what I am doing requires some thought and some grace.

A: Do you play any other sport now?
S: This year no. Last year I played football but at present athletics is my sole sport.

A: What other interests do you have?
S: Theatre, Literature, the papers, dinners with friends, weekends with friends, a few pints, my wife (not in that order'.).

A: Do you have any regrets about being so involved in athletics?
S: Believe it or not I've always taken pains to avoid being involved in athletics to the exclusion of all else. So athletics is just one, albeit important, of the things I do.
I don't regret any part of my athletics career. It has enabled me to meet many people, it's given me self-confidence, self-control and so on, and of course I've enjoyed the glory and respect of others.

A: What are your views on Belgrave Harriers?
S: I think Belgrave's first priority must be to win the Southern League and gain promotion to the National League. This has become an increasingly difficult task and will continue to become more difficult. We shall, if we are not careful, become a club firmly entrenched in the Southern League with little hope of improvement. This will arise because good athletes, and promising athletes, will be attracted to the better competition they will find in the National League. The situation is therefore cumulative, the existing strong clubs will grow stronger and the provincial league clubs, competing with these National League teams in recruitment, will grow weaker until some equilibrium position is reached. The final result might be that clubs relegated from the National League will be too strong for provincial league clubs and therefore will be promoted back to the National League the following year; the population of National League clubs therefore remains fairly stable over a time.
I wouldn't like to generalise too much in this respect. There are and will be provincial league clubs who will rise to National League standard and prosper. As examples of these we have Borough of Enfield, Essex Beagles, Metropolitan Police, Oxford City A.C., in the future perhaps Windsor, Slough and Eton and Haringey. But these clubs all have special characteristics not possessed by Belgrave: (i) a single readily identifiable area from which to recruit, very often with no competing clubs in the same area (Oxford City, Metropolitan Police, Windsor, Slough and Eton), (ii) a tartan track which has provided a focal point to the club, which is why I rate the prospects of Haringey and Windsor rather highly.
Belgrave, on the other hand, has a catchment area which stretches over the whole of South London and competes for recruitment with many other South London clubs. Although Belgrave Hall provides some sort of focal point it benefits mainly cross country and road runners and anyway its attraction must be weakened by having club members so diversified geographically. This makes it difficult for a large percentage of the club to get to and train at the Hall at the same time. I would therefore include Belgrave (potentially, if not yet) with clubs like Herne Hill Harriers, South London Harriers, Surrey A.C., Queens Park Harriers, Hercules-Wimbledon. All these clubs hardly inspire hope for the future and appear, if anything, to be on the wane as far as competitive results are concerned.
I am informed that Belgrave has the athletes - if only they would turn out'. - I have been told this since the Southern League was formed. Belgrave, I was assured, were still a great club, just wait till next year, and if only so many athletes weren't on holiday or in the army and posted elsewhere, or else just couldn't be bothered, we would win the Southern League easily. I think we are still deluding ourselves. In the last Belgravian we were congratulating ourselves for being the best club in Surrey. How can we honestly regard this as a success when we still haven't won the Southern League. And if we do regard this as a success then I think our standards are ashamedly low; how can we, in all conscience, encourage a promising youngster to join us when all we can offer is success in Surrey, surely if we are interested in his development we would rather prefer to divert him to Thames Valley Harriers or Croydon Harriers or Enfield where he would find better competition.
I think that if we are still potentially National League calibre, all those holidaymakers and couldn't be bothered athletes should be pressed to turn out now, because if we wait we will not even have the expectation of good results, the current athlete will have retired and the good youngster will have gone elsewhere. But if the malaise is more fundamental, as it probably is, then we must look for more fundamental solutions. I would favour amalgamations. There are too many clubs in South London. Talent is diluted too thinly and consequently good athletes are condemned to Southern League competition indefinitely. I think that serious consideration should be given to a more rational athletics set-up in South London so that we can eliminate petty squabbles between clubs about who uses which track and who has prior claim on a local youngster. I appreciate that there will be serious opposition to such changes. Many of the South London clubs are the oldest in the country and have long and admired traditions. Also Belgrave Harriers has one of the finest social set ups of any athletic club with its dances and socials and club magazine. I recognise all this and would hate to see it jeopardised. Moreover, the Southern League isn't such a bad league. In some ways, it is preferable to the National League as you compete against different clubs each time out and the atmosphere is more relaxed. Again I accept this and have personally enjoyed the Southern League a great deal. However, unless there is some attempt to win the league and to get into the National League one of the most fundamental drives of athletics is denied - the will to win. If this is missing in Belgrave, and we don't want to get into the National League, then we might as well become a successful social club and forget about athletics.
Finally, if we did have bigger clubs and a Belgrave team in the National League, it would still be possible by some adjustment to the existing rules, to run 'B' sides in the provincial leagues. Thus you have a club catering for all levels of ability and providing a means for the athlete who ceases to be good enough for the National League to continue with his athletics with the same club at a lower level.
I am sorry for the length of this answer, but it really has been frustrating getting nowhere in the Southern League over the years; I'm afraid nothing less than winning or coming second will give us access to the National League. The alternative is not encouraging.

items.heading: ROAD AND COUNTRY
items.byline: GORDON BISCOE Road Running and Cross Country Secretary.
items.summary: Road Running and Cross Country Secretary Gordon Biscoe regrets last season's results and low turn-outs and announces a new points competition for road and cross country members, with its scoring rules.
items.text:
As the records now show, our cross country and road performances last season were not very exciting to say the least. Second place in the Surrey C.C.Champs. and the performance in our own 12 stage road relay being probably our proudest boast. As has now been stated many times it is important that in the next few seasons we must find new talent to take over from some of our more 'ageing' members, either by developing them through our junior ranks and/or from recruiting new members.

However, apart from our need for new stars what was perhaps more disappointing last season was the general low turn-out at all levels in just normal inter-club events as well as Club championships. Due, it appears, generally to apathy and the non-desire to travel to away matches in preference to counter attractions!

In order to give a new look to some of our traditional fixtures and maybe inject a little incentive, a bit more club spirit and teamwork once again, it has been decided for the coming season to introduce a points competition This will cover a number of selected races which will be indicated in the forthcoming fixture list.

The basis of this competition is not new and has, in a similar form, been run effectively by one of our Surrey rivals for some years. The rules of the competition are detailed below and it is intended that for this season (Sept - April) it will be treated as a pilot scheme and depending upon its success any modifications needed will be made for following years.

The prize for this competition will be to the value of £10 and of the winners own choosing. Other prizes may be awarded as is felt necessary. It should be noted that this competition in no way affects handicap prizes or medals etc awarded for any individual Club championship.

May I request that all cross country and road runners help to make this scheme a success but more than this, that in the coming season they will endeavour to make Belgrave a success, especially when selected for representative teams. (Special dispensation will be arranged for those gaining international representation!!)

ROAD RUNNING AND CROSS COUNTRY POINTS COMPETITION.

Points will be scored as follows:

1. In any designated inter-club match open to all members,
a) the first 12 members to finish - 6 points.
b) the next 12 members i.e. 13 - 24 - 5 points.
c) the next 12 members i.e. 25 - 36 - 4 points.
d) the remainder who complete the course - 3 points.

2. In any Club championship,
a) members whose positions in the championship are within the first third of the total number of starters. - 5 points.
b) members within the second third - 4 points.
c) the remainder who complete the course - 3 points.

3. All members actually coming under starters orders in the races designated, irrespective of whether finishing or not, will score 1 point.

4. For acting as a recognised official, course marker or pointsman - 2 points.

The competition is open to all junior and senior members, both first and second claim.
In the case of road relays, points will be awarded as in (2) above except that times will be considered instead of positions.
In the event of any dispute the decision of the Belgrave Committee will be final.

GORDON BISCOE Road Running and Cross Country Secretary.

items.heading: WE WIN OUR OWN & SURREY 20 MILE ROAD RACE
items.summary: Report and results of the Belgrave Open 20 Mile Road Race at Wimbledon on 20 July 1974, won by Bob Atkinson of Cardiff, with Belgrave winning the open team race and the Surrey Championship team race; the text spells Stuart Barratt and the results S.Barrett.
items.text:
JULY 20th 1974 - WIMBLEDON - BELGRAVE OPEN 20 MILE ROAD RACE.

On a hot and humid afternoon and without a single Belgrave vest in our scoring team (is this a record?) we won the open team race from Cardiff and T.V.H., and the Surrey County team race from Epsom & Ewell and Croydon In fairness to our scoring men, however, it was probably just as well that they wore the lightweight white string vests rather than the heavier club vests since in common with other competitors they were denied the refreshment station we should have had along the Kingston by-pass as there were simply insufficient helpers for us to man it. With the aid of helpers from Mitcham and Hercules we managed to have sufficient (just!) pointsmen and helpers. The Club is indebted to the few regular helpers who did turn up.

D.Patterson of T.V.H. led at 5 miles by 13 seconds from Bob Atkinson (Cardiff) and Bill Weller, and by 10 miles had increased his lead to 76 seconds. However, by 15 miles Bob Atkinson was in the lead by 14 seconds from Bill Weller who was in turn 44 seconds up on Patterson. Lionel Mann and Pat O'Connor were running strongly well up the field and although Atkinson increased his lead to win and the second Cardiff man D.Jones was 4th, Bels. ran out winners by 5 points.

Bill Weller won the Surrey race held in conjunction with Pat O'Connor 2nd. With Stuart Barratt in support we just won the Surrey team race by one point.

All in all a good afternoon for our runners but an embarrassment to a club of our size that we had to rely on outside help for one of our major promotions of the year.

DEREK CROOKES

items.heading: ROAD ROUND-UP
items.summary: Round-up of Belgrave runners' performances in road races from April to July 1974, including the Isle of Wight Marathon, Hanwell Carnival 5, Horsham 10 and Lionel Mann's win in the Bedfordshire 10 mile championship.
items.text:
In the Maidenhead 10 miles, back in April, Lionel Mann was well up the field with 5th place in 53:29. Stuart Barrett just missed the hour with 60:12 (56th) and George Piddington clocked 67:31 (67th).

The Isle of Wight Marathon is always a tough event. This year's race in May took place on a very hot day when only the first 21 beat 3 hours. Paul Pringle's 2:53:58 (16th) was excellent. George (52nd) reached the finish in 3:56:47 having taken 68 minutes for the last six miles!

You can't keep old George down though. Nine days later he lined up with Lionel and Trevor Hart for the Aldershot 6-miler. Lionel (2nd) and Trevor (3rd) had a close race, finishing only 4 secs. apart with 31:52 and 31:56. George (41st) completed the team with 40:22 and gave us 4th place just missing the prizes by 1 point.

What a lad he is! Another week goes by and on June 1st George picks a very hot day for his annual pilgrimage to Hull, to fly the Belgrave flag in a 20 mile road race. Only the first two home beat 2 hours and our man was timed at 2:34:11 (32nd).

Bill Weller, limbering up for the Belgrave '20', led home our team in the Hanwell Carnival '5' with 24:50 (3rd). Pat O'Connor wasn't far behind - 26:09 (10th), and the Bels. closed in 2nd team behind Shaftesbury H. On the same day the Fleet '4' gave Derek Crookes 21:45 (31st), George 23:53 (51st) and Ron Langheim 31:09 (64th) the chance to flex their muscles. Good to see you competing again Ron - at least it made a pleasant change for George to have another Belgravian behind him for once!+@'+

June 23rd, and over at Grays in the Thurrock 10 mile race Bill paced out a respectable 49:51 (4th). He gained another 4th with 66:59 on July 7th in the Welwyn Half Marathon, won by Kirkham of Coventry. Pat 70:48 (16th), Lionel 71:41 (21st) and Doug Maughan 77:15 (62nd) gave us another 2nd team place behind TVH.

Sweet revenge came for Pat O'Connor in the Horsham '10' when he beat Trevor Hart who had gained an earlier victory in the Chichester to Portsmouth race. Pat was 12th in 52:55, with Trevor 53:39 (15th), Paul Pringle 58:57 (46th), Stu' Barrett 63:11 (77th), the ubiquitous George 65:05 (87th) Don Bonsor 65:29 (89th), and we finished 4th as a team.

The following day, June 14th, Lionel waged a lonely battle against mainly Luton United runners to win the Bedfordshire 10 mile championship. He finished 26 secs. clear of the field in 52:19.

Glen Haszard who recently joined us and comes from New Zealand, ran in conditions more suited to his homeland when he tackled the Chigwell '10'. In 80F degrees over a very hilly course he pulled through the field well in the second five miles to finish in 61:03 (22nd). Doug. Maughan finished 27th in 61:48, hot and tired.

items.heading: HEROIC RUN BY JOHN BAKER
items.summary: Light-hearted tribute to Hon. Treasurer John Baker, aged 50, who covered 30 miles around Richmond Park in an Esso sponsored run/walk raising £138 for a kidney machine for Charing Cross Hospital.
items.text:
John Baker, our 50 year old Hon. Treasurer, has been the butt of many a jest regarding his un-athletic appearance. Looking like an emaciated version of West German international Harald Norpoth, he lurks near the back of our road and country races, eagerly waiting to pounce like death upon any runner who should get within his range.

The writer will remember to his last days the terror that struck him one murky Saturday in mid-winter. In the gathering dusk on the last lap of the Club '10' he entered the woods with all strength rapidly failing and John Baker behind in full cry. The wail of the banshees could be heard, the harsh panting of tortured lungs getting closer and closer ... until ... he could struggle no more, and he too fell prey to the grey ghost of Belgrave.

We in Belgrave know that beneath John's fragile frame burns a determination that is matchless but one can well imagine the disbelief expressed by his fellow employees at Esso - "What, you a runner!" .

Well, they are regarding John with awesome respect now. You see, a sponsored run/walk was organised by the Esso folk, to raise money to buy a kidney machine for Charing Cross Hospital. John had no problem in gaining sponsors, for after all, surely a bloke like him wouldn't last a mile!

The event took place around Richmond Park, a favourite haunt of our hero. After 30 magnificent miles he wanted to go on and on but Mrs. Veronica Charles, one of the organizers, insisted that John called it a day. He was tired but was in no trouble with his health and doubtless he could have gone on all week. No, it was his poor sponsors that needed protection. They had already been skinned to the tune of £138 by John's efforts and if someone hadn't stepped in they would be working off their debt for another year!

One sour footnote was that one of his sponsors refused to pay up on the grounds that he just did not believe it.

Great work John.

ARM

items.summary: Walking section notes on the summer season: veterans' team placings, Belgrave's improved standing in the 'Nationals' table, Bob Farley leaving for Saudi Arabia, and news of Allan Callow and Dave De Bondi.
items.text:
The summer season has passed and left behind its mark of success and failures. Without doubt much of the credit for placings in some of the races must go to our 'veterans'. John Bromley gave us 2nd team in the Leicester Mercury, Dave McMullen, 2nd team Lambeth, and Bob Farley, winning team Hastings to Brighton. We pulled up well to be 2nd team in the National 50km after a bad one in the '20'.

However, despite our bad ones, we have moved up in the 'Nationals' table from last year's position but this was due to our turning out a team in the Junior Championship last October. With now three active walkers in each age group, Junior and Youths, plus two in the Boys, there is every hope of having teams in this year's 'Nationals' at Chelmsford in October.

On a farewell note, Bob Farley is off to Saudi Arabia for a two year term as a University Lecturer. Bob, who had a quiet period as a result of a knee operation, has fought back well to regain his team position in the longer races. This again leaves our team depleted, especially following Allan Callow's departure mentioned in the previous issue.

News from overseas indicates that Allan has settled in to his new abode and Dave De Bondi is changing status at last. He is marrying a physiotherapist who one hopes will speed Dave up.

CARL LAWTON

items.summary: Report and results of the National 20 miles walk at Redditch on 15 June 1974, run in oppressive heat and won by R.Thorpe of Sheffield, with Belgrave 6th team; it recalls Belgrave's 13 team wins in the championship and the Nijmegen Shield.
items.text:
JUNE 15th 1974 - REDDITCH.

The day was oppressively warm with the sun breaking through to full strength for the last 90 minutes of the race, making it wonderful for supporters but one of extreme difficulty for the competitors. The strength sapping humidity and deceivingly difficult course lured many to over-reach and fall by the wayside, including our own Carl Lawton from whom we have come to expect so much. Ray Middleton with his vast experience gave his usual sterling performance while Ray Hall, but a shadow of his old self, showed it was possible to work through the field and achieve a respectable position.

John Moullin, John Dunsford and Dave King who made up our scoring team deserve praise but to win the 'Blue Riband', the oldest of the Road Walking Championships requires an utter dedication to training and team work. It is a subject for discussion and reflection on 'How best achieved under present conditions'.

It is possibly nostalgia but I recall we have won this team championship 13 times and placed 26 times since the inception 55 years ago of this 20 miles National competition and my feelings yearn for a return to the fitness and comradeship which resulted from the Saturday training sessions round Richmond Park, the laps of the Bridges from Battersea Park, during the mid-week and all-day strolls on a Sunday.

In addition to the four-a-side Championship the 'Nijmegen Shield' for the first club to finish eight men is an important feature of this

National 20 miles Championship continued .....

event and for many years it was a foregone conclusion that we would win this coveted award. Alas, it is many years since we were able to argue who would take it home, or finish a complete team.

Enough of looking back. Sincere thanks to the Midland Counties for an extremely well organised Championship and to our own officials who travelled to Redditch and played a major role as recorders and judges.

JULY 20th 1974 - HENDON - R.W.A. NATIONAL 50 Km.

The Championship was the responsibility of the Southern Area of the R.W.A., and any who have ever assisted in finding a good, safe, sporting course with easy travelling facilities for competitors from all parts of the country, with all the refreshments and other needs required for a race of over 30 miles, will know how formidible was the task.

In no small part the original thinking of Ray Middleton devised a 10 lap course from Copthall Stadium, Hendon which amply met these requirements and enabled spectators, attendants and competitors to give of their best to achieve individual and team honours.

My own observation is that the venue has great possibilities for events of a similar nature.

The day was warm and Carl Lawton sensible to his responsibilities started steadily, moving in that immaculate easy style that at 20 miles one could picture him going to the front. This was not to be, fatigue suddenly struck him and the last two laps were an illustration of his doggedness to finish and complete our team.

As for so many years Ray Middleton came through to lead our team home and with John Moullin and Dave King we finished an honourable second.

The energy of the whole Middleton family must be commented on. Their name is synonymous with "Belgrave Harriers". Jean and her daughters organised raffles which I understand more or less covered the costs of the championship and few people realise the work they do. Congratulations.

AUGUST 10th 1974 - HASTINGS.

The weather forecast was showers or longer outbreaks of rain, thunder at times, gale force gusts of winds from the West, with sunny intervals. How right they were. The fight of competitors along Hastings front to start the 38 miles trek. Thunder, lightning, torrential rain at about 14 miles, then in line with the famous nursery rhyme, "Out came the sunshine", when the South Downs and the countryside displayed all the beauty and lushness which makes one say "This England".

Through-out our men fought the elements and at 20 miles had clearly established themselves, leading in the individual and team championship. A further check between Lewes and Falmer showed Carl Lawton with an 100 yards advantage over Ray Middleton, with Carl Walking with fine style and and confidence of the champion that we know he is. Both had a five minutes lead over the next man. Our team was well placed.

How surprised on arriving at Brighton to find Ray had beaten Carl by over two minutes. Ray's record over the past 10 - 20 years is awesome, astounding and must be unsurpassed in Club history. Congratulations to the remainder of the team.

SEPTEMBER 10th 1949

In the London to Brighton walk on September 10th, eleven of our walkers started off on the stroke of Big Ben at seven o'clock, to be joined later by a number of supporters. In the early stages, Jack Bidgood Bert Clayton, Jack Baker, Jack Wakeley and George Oliver, walked in a group with Don Heath and Joe Wilson not far away. Gordon Doubleday, F.Herring, Sid Spencer and Bill Urry followed at an easier pace.

Jack Bidgood eventually went away from the others and at Chequers Horley was in 9th position. A check at Crawley (29¾ miles) showed that our men had held their positions with the exception of Jack Wakeley who had stopped for a massage. By the time Bolney was reached, Jack Bidgood had improved his position to 7th, Clayton was 16th, Baker 21st and Wilson 27th. With the retirement of Bert Martineau from the Surrey team there seemed a chance that our team would be placed and although Jack Bidgood dropped a couple of places to go back to 9th, Joe Wilson moved up to 23rd and at the finish our positions were: Jack Bidgood 9th; Bert Clayton 16th; Joe Wilson 21st; Jack Baker 23rd making a score of 62 points and just losing us the third position. So Jack Bidgood became our long-distance champion as well as holder of the 20 miles Championship. He's a champion to be proud of. His judgement of pace and unflagging stamina throughout the race set a fine example. Bert Clayton was a worthy second and showed his grit in overcoming tiredness in the last few miles. Joe Wilson walked his best Brighton to date and came along in fine style in the latter half to finish remarkably fresh. Jack Baker pluckily stuck it out over the last half to complete the team.

and 40 years ago

NOVEMBER 1934 - CRAZY CABARET.

The second Social of the Season was held on November 3rd, and was well supported by our guests, Croydon H., Epsom H., and Mitcham A.C., supplemented by the ladies who had been running from the Windmill during the afternoon.

No doubt the advertised Crazy Cabaret, produced by Tom Cotton and trained by Miss Jo Parsons, was one of the attractions, and accounted for the really fine crowd which assembled.

The versatile talent among the Bels. is outstanding! Among the performers were several who have delighted us before, including Tom Cotton, Florrie Footer (once again in the role of Princess Charming), and our old friends Castor and Oil, who again left us without a leg to stand on.

The curtain rose at 9 pm with Miss Gladys Bailey singing "Over My Shoulder", which served to introduce us to "The Seven Belgrave Sisters" (including sylph-like Sidney and Harley, the original Harlequin) in a singing and dancing act which was well received.

Then followed Castor and Oil (alias T.Carter and P.Donnelly, or vice versa. Which is vice and vich is versa, I'll leave you to guess). Their act was very moving. Tom, girlishly garbed in a shimmering creation of russet and gold which displayed her form (or that which he used in lieu of) to advantage, and with lovelight in her eyes, although a trifle haughty as becomes such a queenly figure, was soon swept off her feet by the advances of Paddy, all sackcloth and gnashes. Eventually her feminine charm, plus a half-nelson, brought the debonair swain grovelling at her feet, only to be left flat for his pains! Curtain, amidst tremendous applause.

The ballet opened with Tom Cotton singing.......

.....Love in Bloom appeared from the flower pot in the form of Footer in a blonde wig, garlanded with yellow pansies and little else. Around the hall he scampered, followed by the corps-de-ballet, spraying the audience with sweet scents and Mitcham Lavender........

Altogether a most successful show!

The Youths Medal Competition was neatly sewn up by Peter Crosbie who warily steered clear of the long track races but scored heavily in the field and sprint events to pick up the maximum 100 points for five events. Paul Warren and Danny Richards provided the other medallists with Adrian Cook and David Didino not competing in the necessary five events but nevertheless putting up some good performances.

This year's Boys Competition for the Mrs. L. Ryan Cup turned out to be the most exciting on record. With no less than 45 boys taking part it was a major achievement to score in the necessary five events.

When the day for the last three events arrived everything was set for a close finish. Mark Shippen, the leader after five events, was unable to improve any more as he was away on holiday; Martin Munro who scored max. points on the first two events and was then unable to attend for the next three was back in contention; Simon Shanks had scored well in three events but now desperately needed two more good scores; Ivan Beaumont, older than most of the others and therefore suffering with a lot less handicap allowance; all were pushing for the lead.

The 1,500 metres was Simon's strong point and he scored well, finishing just behind Tony Pilcher and new member J.Heath. Ivan Beaumont leapt a tremendous 15'10" to win the long jump outright and also gained 2nd in the high jump but was it enough? All the time Martin Munro was creeping up with really solid all-round performances.

Working out all the scores for such a close competition was a real headache and after checking and re-checking, Simon Shanks was declared the winner, only 1½ points ahead of Martin Munro who was in turn 5½ up on Ivan Beaumont. The medal for the best score outside the first three in all eight events was won by Stephen Fletcher with a tough all-round performance and not so far behind him came Andrew Byrne who won a special medal. Andrew has improved dramatically in the last twelve months, proving that no matter how far behind you are now, determination plus the strength you gain each year can make all the difference. The losers today can be tomorrow's winners.

A final word of congratulation must go to those mighty "micro-colts" who competed so doggedly against boys considerably older than themselves - David Hicks, David Worley, Andrew Vallance and not forgetting Philip Headley who at eight years old and with only the same allowance as twelve year olds finished a magnificent 4th in the 1,500 metres with an actual time of 5 minutes 48 seconds!

A youngster who has started his athletics with a bang is 12 year old Tony Pilcher. Tony has only been running for a couple of months, having joined the Club after a visit to one of our jumble sales, but already he has set new figures for the junior boys 800 metres and has equalled the 1,500 metre record.

His best 800 metre run came in the Brighton young athletes meeting where he burst from the pack with well over half a lap to go and then kept it up to the finish to win in 2:31.4. This scorching finish has become his trademark and it is a surprise to hear him say, "I don't like 800 metres, it's too far. I really like the 100 metres."

Tony goes to Bushey School at Raynes Park. He gets plenty of sporting encouragement at home from his father, Reg., a keen veteran cyclist who competes for the 29th Wheelers based in Tooting. Reg. has become a most welcome helper when it comes to measuring long jumps etc.

At the moment Tony trains once a week on Sundays at Wimbledon Park. This coming winter he hopes to attend the Friday night sessions at Belgrave Hall as well as continuing his other sporting interest - football. He plays little league football for the Barclay Savers and Oakway teams.

items.heading: CLUB CHAMPIONSHIPS
items.summary: Report on the Belgrave Club Championships back at Battersea Park, with its new all-weather jumping surfaces, covering boys', colts' and senior events and records by Ivan Beaumont, Philip Clay and Stephen W. Crosbie.
items.text:
The return of the Belgrave Club Championships to their historical home of Battersea Park coincided with the all-weather jumping surfaces at that venue becoming available for the first time. A fair number of senior athletes took part, but the most pleasing thing was to see the ranks of youngsters who keenly contested the boys and colts events with heats necessary in both age groups for the 100 metres. So often boys events are held separately from senior competitions, but mixing with the old'ns and simply competing at the same track on the same afternoon seemed to raise their enjoyment of the proceedings. The organisation ran as sweetly as ever and we must thank our visiting officials - Harry Hathway, 'Tommy' Thomas, Mrs Nightingale and Mr and Mrs Long - who did great work in the timekeeping department.

The jumping events produced some excellent performances. Outstanding was the triple jumping of 14 year old Ivan Beaumont who gained 2nd in the senior competition with a distance that beat his own boys record. (Here it must be noted that the following week at Battersea he pulverised the long jump record as well. It had stood since 1961!) Reg. Hopkins, having spent a fortune by entering practically every event, had an exciting duel in the long jump with Snowy Brooks, with the former just getting the verdict with a personal best leap. He also won the high jump, a mere centimetre below the championship best. The junior high jump gave David Didino the chance to launch himself to a new height of 1.67m and Richard Danpure, a new signing, set a championship best in winning the boys event. Philip Clay smashed the previous junior boys club record by 7 centimetres in this event. Richard completed an unusual double by taking his 800 metre race as well. Yes, those jumping areas are going to be a real boon.

Colin Pearson seems to be the eternal runner-up. He has run in Club Championships from 800 metres to 20 miles, always giving his all, but he has never quite managed to make off with the winners "pot". This year's 800 metres was reckoned to be wide open, although Peter Carton, simply on past performances, was favourite. Could Colin do it? Well, he certainly tried, and maybe he was a shade ahead as he attacked Pete down the final straight but as they crossed the line with Colin wildly lunging forward it was Peter who got the decision. Colin turned the tables on him in the 1,500 metres by producing a do or die burst with a full lap to go. Peter had to give way but Laurie O'Hara was clearly untroubled by such tactics.

Alan Black was in a class of his own in the steeplechase although Leo Coy, reducing his week old best by another 30 seconds, is improving fast these days and looks certain to produce a sub - 10 minute run in the not so distant future.

Mark Shippen won a close boys javelin competition with 3rd placer Stephen W. Crosbie setting a new junior boys record. A titanic struggle took place in the senior javelin between John Martin, the holder, and Snowy Brooks. John must have been fairly sure of keeping his hold on the trophy because he hadn't bothered to clean it up. Snowy managed to wrest it away but John had the last laugh when he won the discus after Snowy produced six no throws!

Snowy admitted later that his start was "a bit naughty" in the 100 metres. He held Charlie Gillett off by a tenth with young Reg. breaking new ground with an 11.6 for third. Charlie later stamped his authority on the 200 and 400 metre fields with a couple of good times considering the dusty condition of the track. Philip Gee added a worthy 2nd in the one lap sprint to his earlier 800 metre third place, and Paul Williamson reaped some of the benefits of consistant training with his effort in the 400 metres. At the start of this season, his first, he clocked 56.6 for the event. He is now down to 52.6.

As shown on this issue's cover, David Bailey led home the field in the senior boys' sprint with some hot opposition breathing down his neck. New member James Heath took the colts' race.

items.heading: TRACK AND FIELD
items.summary: Track Secretary Philip Gee's review of a disappointing 1974 Southern League season, in which Belgrave fell to 11th of 25 clubs, praising reliable and newly emerging team members.
items.text:
What a let down! After finishing 3rd and 4th in the Southern League in 1972 and 1973 respectively, our final place this year was a mediocre 11th (out of 25 clubs). We won our opening fixture but the results of the next three meetings looked like we were aiming for arithmetic progression (or perhaps I mean regression!) - we finished 2nd, 3rd and 4th. Our decline was partly arrested by gaining third place in the penultimate fixture but we finished the season at Wimbledon Park with a 4th place.

In common with many other clubs we do not have an unlimited depth of talent, especially in middle distance events and, therefore, injuries to one or two key men (which has happened this year) are really felt. Life is not made easier by a number of members whose variety of excuses never cease to amaze and depress me.

I only hope that 1974 was a bad year and that everyone will make an effort to support whoever takes on the mantle of Track Secretary in 1975. Division 1 of the Southern League is extremely competitive and it would not take much more of a decline to make Division 2 a real possibility in 1976.

After all that I would like to thank those who have made my job easier by their reliability and willingness to compete. Unfortunately space does not permit me to list them all but Steve White (who travels from Oxford to compete for the club) and Charlie Gillett deserve a mention for their efforts; neither ever seems to have a bad run.

New names have, of course, been seen in the Belgrave team this year; Martin Scott, who after competing very successfully at the beginning of the season unfortunately pulled a muscle (see you next season), Paul Williamson, who has steadily improved his 400 metres time and is now almost a regular in the 4 x 400 metres relay team, Leo Coy, who has found his niche in the team at 3,000 metres Steeplechase. He has only run this event three times but has improved from 10m.44secs. to 10m.5.8secs., and finally, Michael Manning, who although still a Junior has turned out in a couple of 5,000 metres league races and has run very well.

PHILIP GEE Track Secretary

items.heading: 'SNOWY' 3rd IN A.A.A.
items.summary: Report on the AAA Decathlon Championship at Aldersley on 8-9 June 1974, where Snowy (C.) Brooks improved his club record to finish 3rd with 6642 points and Reg Hopkins was 10th with 5537.
items.text:
JUNE 8th/9th 1974 - ALDERSLEY.

Snowy Brooks once again improved his Club record decathlon score, this time by 73 points, when he and Reg Hopkins made the journey to Aldersley to take part in the AAA Decathlon Championship. Reg also increased his best score by 175 points with his finest effort coming in the long jump. With many areas in his scoring open to enormous improvement when compared to his individual performances, he has an exciting future ahead of him in this event.

Taking an early lead in the championship Snowy set up fastest time in the 100 metres, and when he followed this with 2nd in the long jump, 1st in the shot and equal 1st in the 400 metres, it was not surprising that the Belgravian found himself leading the competition at the end of the first day. The second day includes his weaker events and he slipped to 2nd overall, 17 points behind the leader, after the hurdles and discus. A best ever vault of 3.50 metres took him temporarily back into the lead and although he lost ground again in the final two contests he was more than proud of his 3rd place in the AAA Championship with a score that moved him to 7th in the United Kingdom for 1974.

items.heading: WE SINK TO 3rd IN LEAGUE
items.summary: Report and results of the third Southern League match at Sutcliffe Park on 29 June 1974, where Belgrave finished 3rd behind Cambridge Harriers and Shaftesbury Harriers, with spectator Gerry North pressed into running the 1,500 metres.
items.text:
JUNE 29th 1974 - SUTCLIFFE PARK.

Our field events section was boosted for the third match of the series by the appearance of Eric Barker, and with Cliff Brooks reaching top form we gained a double win in the shot putt. Unfortunately only four other individual wins came our way and in some events we were hard pushed to even turn out a team. Gerry North arrived to watch and was pressed into running an unaccustomed 1,500 metres in a pair of borrowed spikes with Lionel Mann, who had already run the 5,000 metres, to keep him company.

Charlie Gillett enjoyed his elevation to 'A' string status, equalling his best 100 metre time and winning the 200 metres. This gave Steve White the chance to have a rest from the short events and tackle the one lap race for a change. The net result was the same as usual with Steve crossing the line first in a most comfortable looking 50.6 seconds.

Both short hurdle races provided easy wins for Belgrave with Paul Whitby aggressively taking the 'A' field apart for a clear 1 second margin of victory and Reg Hopkins doing a similar demolition job in the 'B' race. Brothers Steve and Peter Crosbie again proved their worth by scoring some useful points in the triple jump and javelin.

Overall, however, it was very disappointing to finish behind Cambridge Harriers, who are not so strong these days, and Shaftesbury Harriers who are new arrivals from division two. Even our regular relay wins at the meeting's close did little to salvage our pride.

items.heading: OUR WORST S.LEAGUE EVER
items.summary: Report and results of the Southern League match at Clifton Park, Exeter on 6 July 1974, where an under-strength Belgrave team finished 4th, their lowest ever Southern League placing.
items.text:
JULY 6th 1974 - CLIFTON PARK, EXETER.

If the previous week's performance was bad, this effort was a disaster. A crop of injuries and other commitments reduced the Belgrave team to shreds and although those who did go enjoyed themselves, we sank to our lowest ever placing in the Southern League of 4th. To rub salt into the wound even our local rivals Hercules Wimbledon managed to beat us.

But let us not dwell on the gloomy side. As already mentioned our team was out to enjoy itself and the shortage of men gave most the chance to double up on events or tackle something new.

Our hurdlers were in top shape. Reg Hopkins set up a personal best time to win the opening track event, the 400 metre hurdles, and Paul Whitby followed this with a magnificent first ever attempt at the event in 59.4 after a blistering start. They both went on to win their short hurdle races with Paul reducing his seasonal best to 16.2.

The 800 metres gave us more points than of late with both our men ducking under two minutes for the first time this year and John Stow later followed this with an impressive win in the 1,500 metres.

Charlie Gillett and Philip Gee covered the shorter sprints quite successfully and Paul Williamson made his league debut in the 'B' 400 metres with a good 2nd place. Two youngsters also making promising first appearances were David Didino who reached 3rd in the 'B' high jump, and Michael Manning who gained a similar position in the 5,000 metres. Yet another new face was that of Stephen Hartley who has a lot more triple jumping in him when he gets fitter. In the pole vault Alan Mead started out to 'get a point' and ended up by only narrowly failing at 2.60m.

Covering all the throws between them, Bill Couzens and John Martin still had enough energy to compete with Bob Taylor when it came to repetition beer drinking on the train home to London.

Match Result: 1. Plymouth 124pts; 2. Exeter 117pts; 3. Hercules Wimbledon 107pts; 4. BELGRAVE H 99pts; 5. Medway 89pts.

items.heading: Championship wins by Whitby and Stow
items.summary: Report and results of the club 5000 metres and 110m hurdles championships at Battersea Park on 10 July 1974, won by John Stow (J. Stow) by a whisker from Laurie O'Hara and by Paul Whitby.
items.text:
JULY 10th 1974 - BATTERSEA PARK.

After a day of intermittent rain and beneath a sombre and humid sky, 19 runners moved off to cover the 12½ laps of our annual 5000 metre championship.

Following a brisk, bunched first lap the race soon formed into a pattern of small groups: Black, O'Hara, Stow and Carton in the first group were leading a second of North, Pearson and Mann; while further back a grimacing Clive Shippen was giving his younger rivals Coy, Jardine and Maughan a hard time.

Five laps from home the leading group broke up with Stow and O'Hara leaving Peter Carton and a tiring Alan Black. And with less than a mile to go Gerry North ventured from group two and moved into 4th position.

At the bell Stow and O'Hara were still locked together, their nimble feet almost stride for stride. Only a final last gasp dash in the home straight by the younger man prevented Laurie from annexing the 5000 metres title to the 10,000m he earned in May.

Further back Peter Carton held the bronze position; Clive Shippen reversed his 10,000m position over Leo Coy, as did Doug Jardine over Doug Maughan; Fred Paget finished in a lung-busting dead heat with Derek Crookes and our gallant President brought up the rear.

In the 110m Hurdles Paul Whitby ran in devastating fashion to put up a particularly good time on the Battersea Park cinders and take the championship at his first attempt. Decathlon man Reg Hopkins was 2nd and Ronnie McCrossen snatched a narrow margin over Steve Crosbie for 3rd.

items.text:
JULY 20th 1974 - WIMBLEDON PARK.

Belgrave '20' day, traditionally one of the hottest of the year, turned out to be quite a successful day for the Club. Whilst our road runners up at the Common toiled their way beneath the sun to a team victory and our walkers gained 2nd place in the National R.W.A. 50km, our track and field team reached a creditable 2nd amongst the twelve clubs contesting the 'Brockman Trophy'. Trophy meetings generally do not have the atmosphere that they once generated but the 'Brockman', organised slickly by Herne Hill Harriers is still one of the best track meetings of the summer.

A personal best by Paul Whitby in the high hurdles event took him to just one tenth of a second behind our club record, although he was rather disgruntled with his 2nd place. Paul's progress in the few months we have known him has made him one of the key members of our team.

Five times Charlie Gillett stepped onto the track to race and his record at the end of the day was remarkable. He won both his sprint heats in good times, improved on them again in the finals and then helped our relay team on it's way to 2nd place.

Other highlights included Cliff Brooks' throwing and easy 400 metre hurdles win, Arnold Bentt's triple jump of bang on 13 metres, and a determined recovery by Alan Black after he had fallen very heavily at one of the barriers in the steeplechase whilst starting to pull away from the field.

items.heading: THE '74 LEAGUE CLOSES
items.summary: Report and results of the last Southern League match of 1974 at Wimbledon Park on 17 August, where a weakened Belgrave team finished 4th.
items.text:
AUGUST 17th 1974 - WIMBLEDON PARK.

And so to the last match of the season. There were some marvellous individual performances; our wins in the 100 and 200 metres, Jim Rimmer's return from the wilderness, Pete Carton under 2 minutes, Colin Pearson - a good double performance, another best from Leo Coy, youngsters Ronnie McCrossen and Michael Manning, two very good relay runs, Paul Whitby's hurdles, Paul Williamson's two excellent runs, and of course Snowy's eight events. It's no good though, when two events did not include a Belgrave competitor, and due to holidays and injuries a woefully weak field team found itself outclassed.

items.heading: The proposed 'Alf. Harley' club honours board John Walker writes:-
items.summary: Letter from John Walker opposing the proposed 'Alf. Harley' memorial honours board and suggesting the money go on youngsters, a printed club history, advertising and fewer medals.
items.text:
Dear Editor,

Belgrave Harriers. Quo vadis. Is Belgrave Harriers dying? No. Then why the proposed memorial board? I have seen the cap in hand circular and I believe the sum mentioned, 350 nicker (minimum!) should be spent in a much wiser fashion.

Now, contrary to what some wildly deranged Belgravian may think I aint no lecturer! Either in Big Hall or Belgrave Hall! I feel that something should be done to shove some plasma back into the Bels and that can be done only one way. Not with a board, but with flesh and blood. Youngsters. Here I must pay tribute to men who since the Bels formation have done great work administratively. If it is felt by some that one such person should be especially remembered what better than that his name and memory be given to an event - close to his heart - the tribute being no less sincere than as I understand is being contemplated, by a memorial board.

There is another way to remember the history of Belgrave. How about printing, say, 500 copies of the Bels history, with photos, and selling them? In this way a permanent reference could always be to hand in many homes. I realise a lot of work would be involved but it surely is practical and when the books are sold the club would benefit.

Another venture which I'd support would be to encourage youngsters - early teenagers for example by taking parties of lads on regular training weekends by coach somewhere. Also, I believe, as I understand Bill Laws does, that Belgrave should advertise more than at present. Space should be bought in various newspapers and other media.

Getting back to saving money. Why have medals? Incidentally this aint sour grapes! I know I aint won many. I am serious in the medals suggestion. Today engraving and medals are very expensive.

One other thing. I don't believe our Treasurer is that old that he can't take out several novices on a training run. Naturally I mean male novice runners.

items.heading: ...and Clive Shippen replies
items.summary: Past President Clive Shippen, organiser of the Club Honours Board scheme, replies to John Walker: the board's cost, Alf Harley's unfinished club history, and the state of the young membership.
items.text:
As our Past President Clive Shippen has been responsible for organising the Club Honours Board scheme, and is well qualified to comment on John's other suggestions, we felt it would be of interest to hear his views too.

My first reaction on reading John's letter was, "This is just the sort of man we need on our Committee". Ideas are always welcome and, although many come in for quite a buffeting, it is always of benefit to the Club that they should be debated by a lively Committee. I believe our present Committee to be a lively one and, under Charlie Manning's chairmanship, it has had a good year.

Unfortunately, the large amount of investigation and sub-committee work which precedes a decision is not always common knowledge, but I can assure John that several alternative memorial schemes were discussed at great length over a period of months before a final decision was reached. It may interest him to know that his suggestion was one of those considered.

.... continued on following page

As for the Club Honours Board itself, the cost is now expected to be £80 less than the estimated sum and it is my hope that Club funds will not have to find any of the anticipated £270. The response from Past Presidents, Vice-Presidents and Life Members to my request for them to launch this fund was marvellous and well over half sent in letters applauding the decision.

In the course of a year several hundreds of visitors from all spheres come to our Headquarters and on many occasions I have noticed individuals studying with interest the Ken O'Kell boards listing Past Presidents and Internationals. We cannot expect all outsiders to be fully aware of our history but there is a good chance that many future visitors will leave Belgrave Hall with a better knowledge of our great record.

And it is of that great record that Alf Harley was terribly proud. So much so that he spent a great deal of time collecting together all the information he could find, with a view to writing the book that John Walker would like to see. It was never started, but we discussed it and pooled our researches. I hope to make that book reality, but if it took Blackheath six years to write theirs, ours can hardly be done quicker! As for selling 500 copies and making some money for the Club, my own experience of "The Belgravian" and "Veteris" leads me to doubt whether this could be regarded as a money spinning venture.

Now to the youngsters. John suggests that we shove some plasma back into the Bels. Surely he must have seen the Young Athletes section of the June "Belgravian"? There seemed to be plenty of plasma amongst the 50-odd colts, boys and youths photographed or mentioned in that issue - and as our coach trip to Brighton showed, they can produce some useful results in open competition too. Reg Hopkins and Bill Couzens are principally responsible for the healthy state of our young membership, and although they get some help they could do with a lot more. I am sure that they will both be delighted to hear that John supports this type of venture. Perhaps they will hear from you John. Oh! And by the way - see you at the A.G.M.!

items.heading: Bel's king of the mountains
items.summary: John Blair-Fish's 1974 fell-running season in Scotland and Wales, including the Camethy Hill Race, Manx Mountain Marathon and Ben Lomond, ahead of the Ben Nevis race.
items.text:
John Blair-Fish is still running well over the fells up North. Early season efforts included the Camethy Hill Race where he finished 19th out of 98 competitors over the 9 mile/1,600 feet course in 57 mins. 6 secs., and the Manx Mountain Marathon - which sounds a real killer as it traverses 30 miles/9,000feet - in which he was 12th from 51 in 6hrs. 15mins. in spite of losing three-quarters of an hour and climbing an extra 1,000 feet through an error in navigation.

During the summer he tackled eight more of these 'superman events' in Wales and Scotland, gradually improving his average position, over distances varying from 3 to 17 miles, with climbs being as much as 7,500 feet. (Makes the 'kiss of death' on our 5¾ mile race look a bit weak doesn't it.) A particularly good performance was his 4th in the Ben Lomond 9miles/3,000feet where he crossed the line 4th in 1hr. 15mins.

John has cut back in training in the last few weeks to concentrate on the Ben Nevis race on September 7th. He was 40th last year and looks forward to improving on that.

Good luck to you John. We hope to see you running down South again some day.
